title: Oh, Good, Trump’s Arch Will Store Military-Grade Weapons
summary: Good news! The Arch de Trumph will be weaponized, apparently! It will “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers,” according to the president. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World.” You know, for once, I think the president is right. ...
content:
Good news! The Arch de Trumph will be weaponized, apparently! It will “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers,” according to the president. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World.” You know, for once, I think the president is right. I’m going to go out on a limb and agree that this is the only Memorial Arch Armed With Drones and Snipers around! Just as a Fisher Price Push-Around Buggy With a Nuke on the Back would be the only one of its kind.

Here are some other places I assume they will be putting weapons next.

  1. The Institute of Peace, obviously. This is the last place our adversaries will look!
  2. All horses in equestrian statues will be replaced with Trojan horses, filled with tiny armed men ready to pour out at a moment’s notice.
  3. The National Archives will be filled with deadly lasers, programmed to shoot if anyone gets too close to the Constitution. This will both look intimidating and make the Supreme Court’s decisions seem more correct.  
  4. Tanks at the National Aquarium will be replaced with the other kind of tanks.
  5. Singing the national anthem will cause an actual rocket to fire.
  6. Mount Rushmore. Teddy Roosevelt can now shoot missiles from his eyes. Thomas Jefferson has a machete. George Washington’s nose will release cherry bombs in an ominous, sneeze-like formation. Don’t even ask what Abraham Lincoln is now capable of.
  7. The Statue of Liberty. Drones will fly out of her crown at anyone who dares to approach this nation’s shores, and her non-torch-bearing hand will be armed with an electrified stun glove like the ones being issued to ICE. (The poem will also be removed.)
  8. Every statue of Columbus is now a Tactical MechaColumbus. He’s mad, and he wants his parade back!
  9. The Washington Monument. The top now slides open to allow MechaColumbus to pull out an enormous sword.
  10. The Reflecting Pool. Instead of getting rid of the algae, we will train it in the arts of war.
  11. The World War II Memorial is being reconceptualized with free weapons for visitors to take in case the war breaks out again.
  12. J. D. Vance. His jaw will unhinge to reveal a missile launcher. We dare you not to clap for him now!
  13. The Pentagon. (It’s running low!)

title: Don Jr.’s Wedding Trap
summary: If you were a Russian intelligence operative trying to penetrate the American president’s inner circle, you could hardly have done much better than Umar Kremlev did last May. Kremlev, a boxing promoter from outside Moscow, rented a private island in the Bahamas for Donald Trump Jr. to host his uber-...
content:
If you were a Russian intelligence operative trying to penetrate the American president’s inner circle, you could hardly have done much better than Umar Kremlev did last May. Kremlev, a boxing promoter from outside Moscow, rented a private island in the Bahamas for Donald Trump Jr. to host his uber-luxe wedding celebration. Four of President Trump’s children, along with their spouses, were sequestered with Kremlev and a gaggle of other Russians during a party that went on for three days, according to an investigation by ProPublica published last week.

The guest list of family and close friends included the president’s two sons-in-law: Jared Kushner, one of his key interlocutors with Moscow, and Michael Boulos, whose father is a senior adviser to Trump on Arab and Middle Eastern Affairs. A VIP party like that is what spies call a target-rich environment. “It’s an intelligence service’s dream to have so much time with these people, when alcohol is flowing and people’s guards are down,” Marc Polymeropoulos, who used to oversee the CIA’s clandestine operations in Russia, told me. When foreign agents gain access to such a setting, he said, “they are building relationships, gaining assessment data on targets, and perhaps even setting future contact, all precisely part of the recruitment cycle.”

Kremlev shelled out for one night on a private island, as well as a fireworks display, which together can cost upwards of $170,000—a pittance, given the potential payoff. The president, who didn’t attend the wedding, defended the gift, claiming that he, too, had thrown wedding parties for people. “With all of that being said, I understand that Don’s paid him back,” Trump told reporters on Friday, although he didn’t say how much money his son planned to reimburse the Russian. The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia of California, has started an investigation. And yesterday, a Republican senator, John Curtis of Utah, called on his colleagues to investigate the wedding reception and issue a subpoena for Trump Jr.  

Kremlev, who did not respond to a request for comment, has been sanctioned by Ukraine but not by the United States. He owes his position, and apparently his wealth, to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Current and former intelligence officials in the U.S. and Europe who have spent their career working against Russia told me that his gift to Trump’s son should be viewed as the continuation of a long-standing state effort to influence and potentially compromise people in the president’s orbit.

Kremlev, born Umar Lutfulloyev, grew up in a suburb of Moscow and has family roots in Tajikistan. After a few criminal convictions for extortion and battery in the early 2000s, he got into the boxing business. At age 28, Lutfulloyev changed his name to Kremlev, which essentially translates to “the Kremlin’s man.” Around this time, he joined the Night Wolves—ostensibly a patriotic biker gang but really more of a paramilitary and propaganda arm for Putin. The Russian president has previously mounted a bike and joined the gang on rides in the Crimean peninsula, an occupied territory of Ukraine. In 2014, following Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned the Night Wolves, whose members allegedly “conducted intimidation and criminal activities” in the country.

It was in the Night Wolves that Kremlev met Alexey Rubezhnoy, a former member of the FSB, Russia’s main security agency. Rubezhnoy is the current head of the Presidential Security Service, in charge of physical protection for the famously paranoid Russian president. According to Proekt, an independent Russian media outlet that specializes in investigative reporting, Rubezhnoy put Kremlev in position to take over the International Boxing Association, which now serves as an instrument of Russian soft power and a focal point for the Russian government’s rhetorical attacks on LGBTQ people and transgender athletes. Rubenzhnoy also lobbied Putin to nationalize a chain of car dealerships and for Kremlev to lead the company, Proekt reported. The 43-year-old Kremlev is frequently described in the press as an oligarch, a broadly applied term that, if it means anything these days, describes someone who owes his fortunes to the leader of Russia.

Kremlev is just the kind of person the CIA would want to recruit because of his proximity to Putin and Russian state leadership. Yet there he was, ingratiating himself with Trump’s eldest son, who is also a close ally of Vice President Vance and one of the most influential figures on the American political right.

“Espionage is a people business, and access is its holy grail,” John Sipher, a former CIA officer who worked in Moscow and spent his career focused on Russia, told me. Trump Jr.’s Russian guests, he said, had “myriad opportunities for cultivation and exploitation. A shared contact, stray comment, or a business proposition or follow-up meeting can provide information and access that may be leveraged in countless ways.” From the point of view of the U.S. government, which tries to prevent compromising encounters with politically influential Americans, “this is the stuff of counterintelligence nightmares,” Sipher said.

Kremlev’s past and his current connections are well known to the U.S. government and its partners. The Ukrainian government has sanctioned him, citing his close relationship with Putin, Rubezhnoy, and Russian security agencies. Kremlev is also heavily involved with Healthy Fatherland, an organization run by his wife’s twin sister, which Ukraine has sanctioned for its alleged role in the kidnapping and “rehabilitation” of Ukrainian children. A Ukrainian intelligence official told me that its domestic security agency has a thick file on Kremlev. In 2021, for reasons that remain unexplained, U.S. Customs and Border Protection denied a waiver for Kremlev to enter the United States.

[Read: Ukraine’s short-lived comeback]

Before Kremlev took over the boxing association, it was run by Gafur Rakhimov, an Uzbek businessman whom the Treasury Department publicly identified as an organized crime figure in 2012 because of his alleged membership in Brother’s Circle, a Russian criminal network involved in international heroin trafficking. Treasury sanctioned him again five years later for providing material support to another notorious group, Thieves in Law, which originated in Stalinist prison camps in the Soviet Union and is akin to the Italian Cosa Nostra. Rakhimov’s career is a manifestation of the blurry lines in Russia between organized crime, international sports, and the state security apparatus.

The U.S. designations, as well as concerns about the International Boxing Association’s ties to the Russian banking system, prompted the International Olympic Committee to block the association from organizing the sport at the 2020 Tokyo Games. In 2023, USA Boxing withdrew from the IBA, which Kremlev now ran, citing his governmental ties as well as the association’s financial dependency on sanctioned companies. Gazprom, a Russian state-owned energy corporation, had been its largest sponsor.

What Trump Jr. knew about Kremlev’s history is still unknown. When reporters pressed his father, the president suggested that his son “didn’t do a background check.” Within the West Wing, another tough headline elicited some groans and eye rolls, as well as quiet acknowledgment that the ProPublica report would, yet again, spark questions about the relationship between Russia and the Trumps.

For an administration that is generally neither moved nor shamed by questions about ethics, the wedding party triggered a response, albeit a mild one. “I mean, just how dumb can you be?” one outside Trump adviser asked my colleague Jonathan Lemire, on the condition of anonymity so as to not alienate the president's family. One Republican who has been disappointed with the president’s consistent deference to Putin at the expense of Ukraine grimly noted that the wedding had been a savvy play by Moscow to further engender goodwill with the first family. They took this as proof, if any more was needed, that Trump would likely never back Kyiv in the war.

Maybe Trump Jr. didn’t know much about Kremlev. But Russians have long seen Trump Jr. as a conduit to his father, and they have tried to exploit him for political and business purposes.

Back in 2006, Trump Jr. and his sister Ivanka went to Moscow to cultivate potential business contacts. During that trip, a real-estate developer reportedly arranged for Ivanka to sit in Putin’s chair during a tour of the Kremlin. By his own account, Trump Jr. traveled to Russia half a dozen times over the next year and a half. “Russians make up a pretty disproportionate cross section of a lot of our assets,” he said at a real-estate conference in New York in 2008. “We see a lot of money pouring in from Russia,” which he also called a “scary” place to do business.

In 2013, Trump Jr. was the main negotiator on behalf of his father’s company with Russian figures who wanted to construct a Trump-branded tower in Moscow. The deal didn’t materialize, but it laid a foundation for future contacts between the presidential campaign and the Russians that emerged three years later. During the 2016 presidential election, Trump Jr. took a meeting in Trump Tower in New York with Natalia Veselnitskaya, a Russian lawyer who offered incriminating material about Hillary Clinton. When Trump Jr. learned that the Russian might give him dirt on his dad’s opponent, he memorably told an associate, “I love it.” But Veselnitskaya didn’t deliver, and the meeting, in retrospect, looks more like an effort to bring the future president around to pro-Kremlin foreign policy.

[Read: The Qataris gave Trump an airplane. He crippled their country in return.]

When exactly Trump Jr. and Kremlev first met is unclear. The Russian claims it was a couple of years ago. What’s known for sure is that they appeared together on a panel last September at an IBA event in Istanbul. Trump Jr. criticized transgender women and recalled his childhood love of boxing. An appearance onstage by the president’s son and a Russian who’d been sanctioned by Ukraine would not have escaped Moscow’s attention. It was the beginning of an apparent friendship that led to Kremlev subsidizing Trump Jr.’s wedding fete less than a year later.

Kremlev wasn’t the only Russian heavyweight at the party. He was joined by Alexander Lagutin, whom ProPublica described as a businessperson who served in top roles at a Russian defense contractor and a state-backed energy company. Also at the wedding party was Elena Sobol, whom ProPublica called Kremlev’s right hand at the IBA. Sobol didn’t respond to a request for comment, and Lagutin couldn’t be reached.

The attendance of what ProPublica described as a “large contingent” of Russians at a wedding party of only about 50 people was conspicuous. “‘What are they doing here?’ one person recalled thinking,” according to the news organization. After the story was published, Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, acknowledged Kremlev’s largesse, describing it in a social-media post as “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend.” “It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from,” they wrote. “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive.”

Maybe not. But former intelligence officers told me they believe that it’s no mystery why Kremlev was willing to foot the bill for his friends’ big day. “Money motivates—and that generosity can be a means of buying access, cultivating obligation, stealing secrets, and securing influence,” Steven Cash, a former CIA officer who was also the director of the Counterintelligence Program at the Department of Homeland Security, told me. “When the president’s family accepts lavish benefits from someone close to Putin, private financial interests become a national-security concern.”

Kremlev knew what he wanted when he paid for the party. The worrying question now is what Trump Jr. might give him in return.

Jonathan Lemire contributed reporting and Madison Hahamy contributed research to this story.

title: David Ellison Will Get Control of CNN After All
summary: Eighteen months ago, David Ellison was mostly known as an ATM for Hollywood producers seeking to pad out budgets for dad-core flicks such as Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit, Jack Reacher: Never Go Back, and Transformers: Rise of the Beasts. But now, thanks to a timely reallocation of his father’s money, h...
content:
Eighteen months ago, David Ellison was mostly known as an ATM for Hollywood producers seeking to pad out budgets for dad-core flicks such as Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit, Jack Reacher: Never Go Back, and Transformers: Rise of the Beasts. But now, thanks to a timely reallocation of his father’s money, he’s set to be one of the biggest news-media moguls in American history. Having already taken control of CBS News—with little to show for it audience-wise but plenty ideologically—he seems clear to add CNN to his roster of outlets.

His acquisition, through Paramount, of Warner Bros. Discovery has been held up by a lawsuit filed by blue-state attorneys general over antitrust questions. One reported goal of the AGs was to have Ellison sell CNN in order to close the deal, though California’s Rob Bonta labeled that speculation. But yesterday morning, those AGs appeared to give up their fight. As Benjamin Mullin, David McCabe, Shawn Hubler, and Laurel Rosenhall at The New York Times reported:

After weeks of on-again-off-again negotiations, Paramount and the states agreed to a number of concessions to complete the deal, according to the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss details not yet made public. The entertainment giant has agreed to establish a board of journalists to ensure the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News and committed to distributing 30 movies in theaters every year. The company also pledged to spend an additional $1.5 billion on film production over the next five years.

So although another major national news outlet will be under the control of a major Trump ally, at least there’ll be “a board of journalists to ensure the editorial independence”! (That this is happening while the president Ellison supports is banning all CNN reporters from the White House adds a tragicomic veneer to the story.)

If this particular move sounds familiar, that’s because such “boards” have been a part of other news-company acquisitions that have raised similar concerns about antitrust or editorial control. These boards’ effectiveness has been, to be generous, extremely limited. Two of the most prominent examples—both involving Rupert Murdoch—offer little reason for optimism.

[From the April 2025 issue: Growing up Murdoch]

The first began in 1981, when Murdoch wanted to purchase The Times of London and The Sunday Times. The editors of both papers were skeptical. In order to avoid an inquiry by Britain’s antitrust authority, Murdoch agreed to empower a set of “independent national directors” who would have to sign off on the firing or hiring of any top editor, and who would also resolve any major disputes between Murdoch and editors.

In practice, this did not work out. As the legendary editor Harold Evans put it in his 1983 book, Good Times, Bad Times:

[Murdoch had] guaranteed that the editors would have control of the political policy of their newspapers; that they would have freedom within fixed annual budgets; that the editors would not be subject to instruction from either the proprietor or management on the selection and balance of news and opinion; that instructions to journalists would be given only by their editor; and that any future sale of the titles would require the agreement of a majority of the independent national directors. In my year as editor of The Times, Murdoch broke all these guarantees. He put his point of view very simply to the home editor of The Times, Fred Emery, when he summoned him from holiday on 4 March to his office shortly before asking for my resignation: ‘I give instructions to my editors all round the world, why shouldn’t I in London?’

Evans lasted only a year under Murdoch’s ownership. A longer run was had by the conservative editor Andrew Neil, who edited The Sunday Times from 1983 to 1994. Giving parliamentary testimony in 2008, Neil said that the “independence” offered by these outside board members was not about real authority; it was about smoothing the path of an important news outlet into regime-friendly hands:

First of all, let us just remind ourselves. It was a conceit invented by John Biffen and the Thatcher Government to allow Mr. Murdoch to take over these papers in the first place, and it was put in place for that reason. It was not really put in place to protect the independence of the editors.

Neil, arguably the most prominent conservative British journalist of the past half century, was no fellow traveler of the left-wing Guardian, yet he contrasted that paper’s control by the Scott Trust with the kabuki theater of an “independent board”:

The Scott Trust is a perfectly legitimate way of running a newspaper and, as you can see from the success of The Guardian and its on-line success globally, it works. That works. It is entirely different from the strong proprietor who controls the shares and the business of that company appointing a couple of trustees as a fig-leaf.

The second example came in 2007, when Murdoch made an unsolicited offer to the Bancroft family to acquire Dow Jones and its flagship newspaper, The Wall Street Journal. Several family members were concerned about what Murdoch ownership might do to the newspaper’s quality, and as part of the eventual sale, Murdoch agreed to the appointment of a “Dow Jones Special Committee” that would, much like its London predecessor, have final say over the hiring and firing of top editors, as well as changes that could be construed as forcing an editor out.

With that guarantee in place, enough hesitant Bancrofts were persuaded to sell—though not everyone was on board. “Although I’m convinced that News Corp. offer is very generous in financial terms,” Dieter von Holtzbrinck, a Dow Jones director, wrote in his resignation letter, “I’m very worried that Dow Jones unique journalistic values will long-term strongly suffer after the proposed sale.” He added, “I do not believe that the ‘Special Committee’ can finally prevent Mr. Murdoch from doing what he wants to do, from acting his way.”

Barely four months after the transaction closed, he was proved right. Murdoch managed a nifty end run around the “special committee” and ousted the newsroom’s top editor, Marcus Brauchli. Murdoch didn’t fire Brauchli. Instead, he layered over him, naming the former Times of London editor Robert Thomson as publisher, but giving him direct oversight of the newsroom rather than the position’s usual business-side responsibilities. Brauchli, frozen out of major decisions in the newsroom he allegedly led, sent a note to staff saying he had “come to believe the new owners should have a managing editor of their choosing.” Brauchli was well compensated with a nice “consulting” gig for Dow Jones.

Because Brauchli had resigned rather than be fired, the approval of the special committee was not required. Murdoch informed its members as a fait accompli, telling one, “I have no doubt that The New York Times will make trouble with it for a day or two, but I’m not too bothered by it.” The committee later issued a statement in which members “expressed the view that learning of the Brauchli matter after the fact failed to meet the letter and the spirit of the agreement.” But alas, the committee “decided there was no practical way to ‘unresign’ Brauchli and start the process over.”

[David A. Graham: Hindsight is 2024]

The reporter Sarah Ellison (no relation to David), in her book on the Murdoch takeover of the Journal, described the special committee as “an artificial set of rules he would inevitably circumvent,” which seems dead-on.

Right now, we don’t know much about what a CNN (or CBS News) “independent editorial board” will look like. Bloomberg News reports that it “will be composed only of journalists, with no executives or shareholders allowed to join,” and that “the board will be required to have political balance.” The deal does not appear to have any sort of hard enforcement mechanism built in for any violations of the “the letter and the spirit” of the editorial independence agreement. (By contrast, it does include a $30 million penalty for each film Paramount promises to release to theaters but doesn’t.)

But let’s be blunt. No matter how well intentioned the members of these committees may be, if David Ellison wants to get around them, he will. The rules being put in place are an artificial set that a billionaire owner will inevitably circumvent. Such “independent” boards are PR gestures, not vehicles for editorial protection. As Andrew Neil said, they are tools to get a controversial deal across the finish line. And at that, they seem to have succeeded once again.

This post appears courtesy of Nieman Lab.

title: The ‘New Word’ Trump Hates
summary: Of all the outrages and betrayals that Donald Trump has had perpetrated against him—by ungrateful subordinates, by obstreperous prosecutors, by treacherous journalists—perhaps his saddest falling-out is with a simple word. “Starting on day one, we will defeat inflation quickly, and we will make Amer...
content:
Of all the outrages and betrayals that Donald Trump has had perpetrated against him—by ungrateful subordinates, by obstreperous prosecutors, by treacherous journalists—perhaps his saddest falling-out is with a simple word. “Starting on day one, we will defeat inflation quickly, and we will make America affordable again,” he declared in an ad during his 2024 presidential campaign. A year later, Trump confessed to still having some affinity for the word. Speaking at a summit hosted by McDonald’s, the president promised imminent prosperity: “That begins with making America, we have to do—the word is affordable—and affordable should be our word, not theirs.” These days, the word itself is, like all of Trump’s enemies, the frequent target of invective. The president describes the concept of affordability as, variously, a Democratic “con job,” as “a new word—nobody ever heard the word,” and, most damningly of all, as “fake.”

The reasons for this lexical animosity are clear. The word that the president once wielded with great effect against Democrats in 2024 is now being used against him with seemingly equal effect by his opponents. Affordability is the Democrats’ unifying theme, which, despite them lacking coherence on almost every other issue, may be enough to carry them to victory in the November midterm elections. (Nate Silver estimates that in the generic congressional ballot, Democrats are leading by a crushing 7.5 percentage points.) And no wonder. Inflation remains high; gas prices, which Trump promised in 2024 would settle below $2 a gallon, are now above $4 thanks to the president’s war with Iran; mortgage rates, which Trump said would drop to 2 percent, are instead near 7 percent.

[Marc Novicoff: Gas prices could cost Republicans the midterms]

But Democrats shouldn’t expect to hang on to their advantage here; far more likely, the inversion will recur. You can imagine America settling into a persistent politics of affordability, in which the arguments are always the same but the positions of accuser and accused are swapped depending on who holds power. Democrats are, for example, pledging that if they win the midterm elections, they will crusade for lower costs “of groceries, of housing, of childcare and elder care.” Perhaps such competition would be salutary; more likely, it would be Sisyphean—an unending cycle of accusation, disappointment, and recrimination.

There are three reasons for pessimism. The first is that affordability politics are a breeding ground for economically illiterate policy ideas. Popular anger over inflation is usually directed at cumulative price increases over the course of years. But literally decreasing prices is exceptionally hard to accomplish, even if that is what voters want. In this heady environment, discredited ideas such as price controls and even the direct provision of goods—as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is attempting with government-run grocery stores—make their resurgence. Affordability politics also encourages unvarnished attempts at bribing voters, as Trump attempted with his pledge to give $5,000 to every American adult should Republicans keep control of Congress. (This is both a subpar reason to add another $1.3 trillion to America’s $40 trillion in national debt and a very good way to exacerbate inflation.)

[From the August 2026 issue: The ‘consumer socialism’ trap]

The second problem of affordability politics is what these proposed solutions do to what little remains of voter trust in government. Every election cycle, politicians make promises for widespread price relief, package them into neat advertisements, and relay these to voters a mind-numbing number of times, only for these promises to go undelivered—because they were unworkable from the start. This may not inspire apathy among voters so much as anger and irritability. It also encourages anti-incumbency of the kind that explains why Americans have, in every presidential election since 2016, opted for the challenging party’s candidate.

The third problem is the cumulative cost of short-termist affordability politics. Neither party in this election cycle is making much reference to the national debt, even though the United States has surpassed, for the first time ever, $1 trillion in interest costs this year. Deficit spending shows no sign of slowing down, even though the American economy is not in recession and the country is only mildly at war. But there is no political incentive to suggest that such spending cannot persist. Instead, Democrats traditionally propose new social expenditures and subsidies, whereas Republicans propose general tax cuts. The new approach, favored by populists, is to offer both: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for the Senate race in Michigan, has pitched “a cost-of-living exemption on federal taxes up to $50,000” while also establishing Medicare for All and universal child care—to be paid for by the rich. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for the Senate race in Iowa, is pitching more government support for house purchases, child care, and rural hospitals while cutting taxes.

Why begrudge the entire enterprise of affordability politicking? Isn’t the job of elected officials ostensibly to improve the lives of their constituents? Yes, indeed. And it is of course still possible to durably decrease prices with good governmental policy: You can, for example, slowly reduce the cost of housing by reducing restrictions on building, or reduce health costs by expanding the supply of doctors. This requires some forbearance and sophistication on the part of the politician—and, unfortunately, both qualities are negatively selected against in the current political-attention economy. It is better to make headlines with snappier pledges to freeze the rent or nationalize the health system. You can safely assume that at the conclusion of the midterms, the 2028 presidential election will begin in earnest and affordability will be one of its bywords. You can also dread the litany of bad ideas it will spawn.

title: America’s Biggest Dating Company Is Betting on Trad Values
summary: If a dating app existed in the 1950s, you might expect it to look like Upward. On “chivalry mode,” users can establish that the man in a straight pairing will message the woman first. With “marriage timeline,” they can specify how soon they’d like to marry. In one promotional image, a man leans agai...
content:
If a dating app existed in the 1950s, you might expect it to look like Upward. On “chivalry mode,” users can establish that the man in a straight pairing will message the woman first. With “marriage timeline,” they can specify how soon they’d like to marry. In one promotional image, a man leans against a car; below him is the caption “Known to change a tire, not his feelings for you.” In another, a man smiles, coffee cup in hand: “Known to cover the reservation and the check.” A woman in a cowboy hat is “often described as wifey material.”

This is not, in fact, a glitch in the time-space continuum, the 20th century folding in on the 21st. It’s the newest big project for Match Group, the company that owns an abundance of dating apps, including Hinge and Tinder. Today, Match relaunched Upward, formerly a Christian dating app but now a home for anybody who wants to settle down—the old-fashioned way. “This is modern courtship in action,” the company’s press release reads. “Women are clear about their standards, men pursue with purpose, and both move toward marriage together.”

[Read: The great romance slump]

Any number of other platforms let you date with the purpose of getting hitched, of course. On Hinge or Tinder or Bumble, you can indicate what type of relationship you’re looking for and whether you want children. I see plenty of people on dating apps openly calling for a soulmate, a spouse, a co-parent—and I’m in New York City, not Tuscaloosa. What Match is capitalizing on, though, isn’t simply a yearning for matrimony or parenthood. It’s leveraging what’s arguably a regressive streak in the culture: a tendency to romanticize the scripts that more Americans used to follow, which told them how men and women should behave and what they should value. Internally, Match calls Upward’s audience the “next-gen traditionalists.” Now the company is betting on them.

About 10 months ago, Match pulled together some data on its apps’ audiences. The one that stood out, surprisingly, was Upward.

The singles using Upward, though they sometimes talked about faith, didn’t overall seem keen to discuss the details of their religious practice. Profile prompts such as “What’s your favorite Bible verse?” weren’t widely used. Match’s chief marketing officer, Stephanie Danzi, told me that instead, the unifying factor appeared to be a specific vision of the future. These people wanted to get married and have kids—not probably or eventually, but seriously and soon. When Match surveyed couples who had met on Upward, they found that the average time from match to marriage was less than a year.

Upward, in other words, looked like an opportunity. Marriage rates have been falling for years, but that doesn’t mean people aren’t hoping to tie the knot. In the Kinsey Institute’s recent 2026 “Singles in America” study, funded by Match, 72 percent of Gen Z participants—more than any other generation—said they want to get married. I’ve seen this in my own reporting: For plenty of people, marriage seems like both a far-off goal and an essential one.

[Read: The unglamorous truth about the average tradwife]

Desiring marriage doesn’t necessarily mean you want to follow strict gender norms. But young people today are veering toward traditionalism; tradwife influencers and manosphere podcasters aren’t the only ones who think that men and women ought to stay in separate lanes. In a global Ipsos poll from last year, about a third of Gen Z men agreed that “a wife should always obey her husband”—more than double the share of Baby Boomer men who said the same. Although only 6 percent of Baby Boomer women affirmed the statement, nearly 20 percent of Gen Z women did. And in that “Singles in America” survey, more than half of respondents—and 70 percent of Gen Z men—said that women should be their children’s primary caregiver, up from 34 percent of respondents in 2013.

Upward is leaning into that shift. In promo videos, a couple who met on the app practices “chivalrymaxxing”: the husband opens a car door for his wife, gives her his jacket, picks her up, and carries her around. (In an especially unsubtle bit of conservative coding, Match mentions that the couple’s first date involved Chick-fil-A.) The press release announcing the relaunch notes that the app’s new design draws from “Americana” and that the tone is “nostalgic.” A quintessential Upward member, Danzi said, might be a young woman looking for a “ring by spring”: She hopes to be engaged by the time she graduates. I thought of the 2003 movie Mona Lisa Smile, which is set in the 1950s. Julia Roberts plays a Wellesley art-history professor who tries to show her students that they can pursue dreams other than marriage. When I watched that as a girl, the idea that women would need this kind of convincing seemed disturbing but blessedly buried in history.   

Danzi didn’t describe Upward as an anti-feminist app—far from it. She explained that many Zoomers find romance confusing and intimidating; sometimes, they know what they want but not how to convey it. With Upward, “the rules of courtship are really clear; the end goal is really clear,” she said. “So you don’t have to deal with the ambiguity of like, I don’t want to come on too strong by saying I want to have four kids or whatever it may be.” And if women say they want to be pursued, if they want to be homemakers, if they want a ring by spring—well, Match is helping them achieve their goals. Upward, Danzi said, is giving people “the agency to go after what’s really important to them.”

[Read: Bumble hands the first move back to men]

Match isn’t the only dating titan to make this argument. The app Bumble, when it launched in 2014, branded itself as a feminist app with the premise that the woman messages the man first. But then the company announced last month that many women no longer want the duty of initiating; men are now allowed to start the conversation. “You have to move with culture, or you get left behind,” the platform’s founder, Whitney Wolfe Herd, said at The Atlantic Festival last week. “You have to listen to data.” Bumble read the winds—and the winds, apparently, were trad.

Modern dating can be complicated in some ways it didn’t used to be. Women have to decide what they want to do with the agency that comes from greater financial power. Men have to consider what they’ll bring to a relationship besides just money in the bank. The cost of choice is responsibility: to comprehend your own complex desires and also to communicate them, which, as Danzi noted, many young adults struggle with. Perhaps that’s partly because dating apps have allowed them to sidestep tricky in-person conversations, to avoid approaching anyone who might not be interested, or to interact without trying very hard at all. Danzi said that Upward is “making effort easy”—but I don’t think that’s how effort works. Now Match and Bumble are justifying their products by pointing to a problem that they helped create.

title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
summary: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violenceTwo men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US depor...
content:
Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.

The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.

content:
Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children

Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna.

The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal goldmines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger.

Four of Nusrat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week

A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.
